text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The Swedish parliament on Thursday passed a government proposal about changed labor market legislation. The proposal, strongly disliked by unions, means rights for employers and unions to strike local deals that diverge somewhat from central agreements. It also contains a new form of employment, allowing companies to hire five people for limited time periods of up to one year.

- Sweden should become more involved in the EU's common defense and security policies, says French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette to the Swedish government in an editorial article. The French aim for closer ties between EU, the WEU and Nato, the paper said. Sweden could be in the inner circle of countries working toward such closer links, Charette said.

- Economists at Swedish umbrella union organisation LO, which historically has supported the Social Democrats, critisises the Social Democratic Finance Minister Erik Asbrink for not boosting growth and creating more jobs, the paper said. Instead, Asbrink is building up a large budget surplus.

- Smuggling rice into Sweden via Norway has increased sharply and customs authorities have confiscated 8.5 tonnes in recent days. Wholesalers and import companies, who sell the rice to restaurants, are suspected of being behind the illegal trade.

- Social Democratic leaders hope worker protests against government policies, which have included large budget cutbacks, will subside after Thursday's passing of new labour market laws. the paper said.
- Computer consulting company Mandator's share issue was oversubscribed 28 times, according to preliminary figures released by Mandator. The issue gave Mandator 50 million crowns.

- Swedish chemicals company Perstorp will sell most of its auto parts operation to Collins & Aikman of North Carolina. Perstorp shares climbed by 6 crowns to 133 crowns on the news that Collins & Aikman will buy the operations of Perstorp's Components Division in North America, the U.K. and Spain for 1.2 billion crowns.

- Danish package tour provider Spies and Tjareberg, which suffered a loss of 225 million Danish crowns in 1995, is looking at a profit this year of 30 million Danish crowns. The Danish air travel firm was acquired on February 15 by Scandinavian Leisure Group, which is in turn owned by Airtours. Thanks partly to the advantages of bigger volumes and an improved Scandinavian travel market, Spies and Tjareborg was already making money in September.
